title: Building and booting a custom kernel

lessons.title: Kernel versions and the release cycle
lessons.goal:
Learn to read a kernel version string, see which kernel packages and boot entries a machine has, and understand how new kernels are released.

Why it matters: "which kernel are we on, and is it supported?" is asked in every incident and every audit.

setup.note: Steps with sudo load a harmless module (`dummy`) and change one sysctl value, then restore both. Use a throwaway machine.

steps.title: Reading uname -r
steps.text: `6.12.0-206.104.4.4.el9uek.aarch64` has: the **upstream version** `6.12.0` (mainline 6.12), the **distribution's build** `206.104.4.4` and its tag `el9uek` (Oracle Linux 9, Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel), and the architecture. Vendors add their own patches on top of the upstream number, so "6.12" does not mean the same code everywhere.

steps.title: Installed kernels and the boot entries
steps.text: Several kernels can be installed side by side. The boot loader menu lists them. The default is what boots next. Keeping the previous one is your fallback.

steps.title: The build configuration of a kernel
steps.text: Every kernel is built with a configuration: thousands of options, each `y` (built in), `m` (module) or not set. The file is stored next to the kernel.

steps.title: The release cycle
steps.text:
Upstream Linux follows a steady rhythm.

- **Merge window** (2 weeks): new features go in, ending with `-rc1`.
- **Release candidates** `-rc2` ... `-rc7` (or rc8), one per week: only fixes.
- **Release**: `6.N` after about 9 to 10 weeks. New releases come about every 9 to 10 weeks.
- **Stable** `6.N.y`: bug fixes for a few months. Some releases become **LTS** (long term support) with years of fixes. Distributions usually base their kernel on an LTS release and backport fixes.

run.reason: the answer changes daily; shown as the command you would run, not recorded

steps.under: Linus Torvalds releases mainline. The first number changes rarely and has no technical meaning (4.20 was followed by 5.0, 5.19 by 6.0). Greg Kroah-Hartman and Sasha Levin maintain the stable trees. Enterprise vendors freeze a version for a release and backport security fixes, so a "5.14" Red Hat kernel can contain code from 6.x.

quiz.q: How long is the usual merge window?
Why keep the old kernel installed after an update?
options: It is the fallback if the new one does not boot
quiz.explain: Choose it in the boot menu if the new kernel fails.

check.scenario: An audit says "your servers run kernel 5.14, which is end of life". They run Oracle/Red Hat kernels. How do you answer?
check.answer: Vendor kernels carry backported fixes, so the upstream number alone is not the support status. Check the vendor's errata and the package release (`rpm -q kernel` / `uname -r`) against their advisories (`dnf updateinfo list security`). The question to answer is whether the **vendor build** is current and within its support window.

lessons.title: Building and booting a custom kernel: the walkthrough
lessons.goal:
Learn the steps to build, install and safely test your own kernel, and how to read the configuration and boot parameters you would change.

Why it matters: you will rarely build a kernel on a production server, but you must understand the pieces (config, image, modules, initramfs, boot entry, fallback) to debug boot problems and to apply patched kernels.

setup.note: Steps with sudo load a harmless module (`dummy`) and change one sysctl value, then restore both. Use a throwaway machine.

steps.title: What a kernel installation consists of
steps.text: Four things must match: the **kernel image** (`vmlinuz-VERSION`), its **modules** (`/lib/modules/VERSION`), an **initramfs** (early user space that can mount the root file system) and a **boot loader entry**.

steps.title: Step 1: get the source and a configuration
steps.text: Start from the configuration of the working kernel and let `olddefconfig` set new options to their defaults. This is much safer than starting from nothing.

run.cmd: curl -O https://cdn.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/v6.x/linux-6.12.tar.xz && tar xf linux-6.12.tar.xz && cd linux-6.12 && cp /boot/config-$(uname -r) .config && make olddefconfig
run.reason: downloads about 140 MB and unpacks 1.5 GB; this VM has little free disk

steps.title: Step 2: build
steps.text: `make -j N` compiles the kernel and `make modules` the modules. Use a unique `LOCALVERSION` so the new modules do not overwrite the old ones.

run.reason: a full build takes hours on this 1-CPU VM and needs several GB of disk

steps.title: Step 3: install
steps.text: `modules_install` copies modules to `/lib/modules/VERSION`. `make install` (or `kernel-install`) copies the image, builds the initramfs with `dracut` and adds a boot entry.

run.cmd: sudo make modules_install && sudo make install
run.reason: installs a kernel into /boot and changes the boot menu of this machine

steps.title: Step 4: boot it once, with a fallback
steps.text: Set the new kernel for the **next boot only** and keep the old one as default. If the new kernel panics, a power cycle returns to the working one.

run.cmd: sudo grubby --set-default /boot/vmlinuz-6.12.0-custom && sudo grub2-reboot 0 && sudo reboot

run.output:
index=0
title="Oracle Linux Server (6.12.0-206.104.4.4.el9uek.aarch64 with Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel) 9.8"

steps.after: The last command lists the first boot entry. `grub2-reboot` selects an entry for a single boot.

steps.title: Boot parameters
steps.text: The command line after the kernel name configures it for one boot: root device, console, quiet. They are visible in `/proc/cmdline`. Edit persistent defaults with `grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=...`.
steps.under: The boot loader loads the kernel image and the initramfs into memory and jumps to the kernel with the command line. The kernel unpacks the initramfs as a temporary root, runs `/init` (systemd in dracut), loads the storage driver, mounts the real root and switches to it (module 24).

quiz.q: Which files must match for a kernel to boot?
options: Image, modules, initramfs and a boot entry

quiz.q: Why start from the existing /boot/config and run `make olddefconfig`?
options: It keeps the options that work on this hardware and sets new ones to defaults
quiz.explain: It starts from a known-good configuration.

quiz.q: How do you try a new kernel once and fall back automatically?
options: grub2-reboot to boot the new entry for one boot
quiz.explain: grub2-reboot (or grubby) sets a one-time entry.

options: Early user space with the drivers needed to mount the root file system
quiz.explain: It lets the kernel reach the real root.

check.scenario: A new kernel panics with `VFS: Unable to mount root fs`. What is the most likely build or install mistake, and how do you recover?
check.answer: The initramfs lacks the storage or file system driver (or was not built for this kernel), or `root=` is wrong. Recover by booting the old kernel from the GRUB menu, then rebuild the initramfs with `dracut --force /boot/initramfs-VERSION.img VERSION` after `depmod`, and check `lsinitrd` for the driver.

interview.q: How do you read a kernel version like 6.12.0-206.el9uek?
interview.a: Upstream base 6.12.0, then the distributor's build number and tag (EL9, UEK). Vendors backport fixes, so the base version alone does not tell the patch level. See [the lesson](#/lesson/14/kernel-versions).
About every 9 to 10 weeks: a 2-week merge window, then rc1..rc7/8 weekly, then the release. Some versions become LTS.

interview.q: What are the steps to build and install a kernel?
interview.a: Get source, start from the current .config and run `make olddefconfig`, `make -j`, `make modules_install`, `make install` (image, initramfs, boot entry), test with a one-time boot, keep the old kernel as fallback. See [the walkthrough](#/lesson/14/custom-kernel).
It is a small root file system loaded by the boot loader. It contains the drivers and tools to find and mount the real root file system, then switches to it.

interview.q: How do you keep a machine bootable when testing a kernel?
interview.a: Keep the working kernel installed, boot the new one once (`grub2-reboot`), have console access, and keep the previous GRUB entry as default.
